intro: Two-sample tests compare two parameters. For two means, $t=\dfrac{(\bar{x}_1-\bar{x}_2)-0}{\sqrt{s_1^2/n_1+s_2^2/n_2}}$ tests $H_0:\mu_1=\mu_2$. For two proportions, a z test uses the combined (pooled) proportion in the standard error under $H_0:p_1=p_2$. A matched-pairs design instead analyzes the differences within pairs with a one-sample t test on those differences. Always state hypotheses, check conditions, compute the statistic and p-value, and conclude in context.

items.prompt: Compute the two-sample t statistic: $\bar{x}_1=20$, $\bar{x}_2=16$, SE of difference $=2$.
When should you use a matched-pairs (one-sample on differences) analysis?

steps: Matched pairs arise when each observation in one group is naturally linked to one in the other.
Then you analyze the within-pair differences.
So use it for paired data (before/after, twins, same subject).
solution.answer: For paired data; analyze the differences with a one-sample t.

items.prompt: For a two-proportion z test, what proportion goes into the null standard error?

steps: Under $H_0:p_1=p_2$, the best estimate is the combined success rate.
That is the pooled proportion $\hat{p}=\frac{\text{total successes}}{\text{total sample}}$.
